steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our survey on federated continual learning viewed as knowledge fusion: why federated learning is needed, its two main challenges, what FCL adds, our contributions, and how the survey is organized.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Deep learning needs centralized data; federated learning as the response
- Challenge 1: lack of dynamism -> temporal catastrophic forgetting
- Challenge 2: data heterogeneity -> spatial catastrophic forgetting
- Federated Continual Learning and spatial-temporal catastrophic forgetting
- This survey: FCL as knowledge fusion; contributions
- Organization of the paper

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- Deep learning and FL
  - deep learning instrumental in data analysis and AI; used in almost all areas of industry, science, engineering
  - needs large training data + centralized training -> often impractical/impossible
  - mobile devices: hard to collect/transfer data to central server with limited bandwidth
  - centralized training infeasible: data privacy, data silos (information security, laws and regulations, competition among technology giants)
  - FL: positive response to need for privacy etc.
  - devices train global model collaboratively, upload models to server, private data stays local
  - involves privacy preservation, knowledge transfer, collaboration among data owners
  - promising results in sensitive-data industries: finance, healthcare, electronic communication, government affairs
- Challenge 1: lack of dynamism
  - most FL methods assume all data and classes known beforehand and unchanged forever
  - real world: data in streams, sequential tasks
  - FL suffers temporal catastrophic forgetting (TemporalCF) on new tasks
  - TemporalCF: major challenge in Continual Learning (CL); crucial parameters of a single model change on consecutive tasks -> poor performance on previous tasks
  - FL clients learning task sequences from local streams will hit TemporalCF
- Challenge 2: data heterogeneity (Non-IID)
  - differences in data distributions, feature spaces, labels across clients; from data sources, collection methods, data quality
  - diverse knowledge in local models; knowledge represented by parameters; more different data -> greater parameter divergence
  - simple aggregation (averaging) overwrites critical parameters -> global model worse than local models on local test set
  - spatial catastrophic forgetting (SpatialCF): new concept from this paper, analogical to TemporalCF
- FCL
  - Federated Continual Learning breaks static limitations of FL; each client learns a task sequence
  - fundamental problem: spatial-temporal catastrophic forgetting
  - clients: TemporalCF from new tasks; server: SpatialCF from aggregation
  - after each task: server aggregates -> global model -> foundation for next task => SpatialCF may exacerbate TemporalCF
- This survey
  - enumerate FCL algorithms, how they overcome spatial/temporal CF or both
  - extensive experiments; FCL training = knowledge fusion (previous + current task; heterogeneous clients)
  - uploading full parameters/gradients: privacy leakage, slow aggregation from communication cost
  - FCL methods: extract knowledge locally, upload extracted knowledge, more efficient aggregation
  - contributions: discuss FCL, spatial-temporal CF, two evaluation metrics, experiments; two unified frameworks (synchronous, asynchronous); survey by seven forms of knowledge fusion (rehearsal, clustering, regularization, parameter isolation, dynamic architecture, prototype, knowledge distillation)
- Organization
  - Sec. II: FL, CL, motivation for FCL
  - Sec. III: spatial-temporal CF, experiments on traditional FL
  - Sec. IV: synchronous and asynchronous FCL frameworks
  - Sec. V: FCL methods by knowledge fusion (rehearsal, clustering, all gradients/parameters, parameter isolation, prototype, dynamic architecture, knowledge distillation)
  - Sec. VI: summary, future directions

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Deep learning has been instrumental in the advances of data analysis and artificial intelligence (AI). The algorithms have been used successfully in almost all application areas in industry, science, and engineering. However, traditional deep learning algorithms usually need large amounts of training data and centralized training, and this is often impractical or even impossible in practice. For example, with mobile devices it is difficult to collect large amounts of data and transfer them to a central server with limited bandwidth. Centralized training is also infeasible because of data privacy and data silos, which come from information security, related laws and regulations, and intensive competition among technology giants. In recent years federated learning (FL) has emerged as a positive response to the increasing need for privacy and other concerns in machine learning applications. In this new paradigm, multiple devices train a global model collaboratively by uploading their models to a server while the private data stays local, instead of the traditional approach with centralized data storage and model training. FL mainly involves privacy preservation, knowledge transfer, and collaboration among data owners, and these are essential for many real-world applications of AI. After several years of development FL has produced promising results, especially in industries that handle sensitive data such as finance, healthcare, electronic communication and government affairs.

FL has many advantages but it also faces significant challenges. The first challenge is that it lacks dynamism. Most existing FL methods make quite strong assumptions, namely that all data and classes are known beforehand and will never change. This contradicts the dynamic nature of the real world, where data is collected in streams and the data can form sequential tasks. But traditional FL would suffer from terrible temporal catastrophic forgetting (TemporalCF) when the local models learn new tasks. TemporalCF is a major challenge in Continual Learning (CL); it refers to changes in crucial parameters of a single model when it learns on consecutive tasks, which leads to poor performance on previous tasks. So FL would certainly run into TemporalCF if each client learns a sequence of tasks from a private local data stream.

Another challenge of FL is data heterogeneity, which is also called non-independent and identically distributed (Non-IID) data. It means the differences in data distributions, feature spaces and labels across the clients in the federated training process, caused by variations in the data sources, data collection methods, data quality, etc. Because of data heterogeneity, the local models extract diverse knowledge. The knowledge of a model is often represented by its parameters, and the more different the data is, the greater the parameter divergence is. If we simply aggregate these local models, for example by averaging parameters, parameters that are critical for some local tasks can be overwritten. So the aggregated global model may perform worse than the local models on the local test set. We call this phenomenon spatial catastrophic forgetting (SpatialCF). SpatialCF is a new concept that we introduce in this paper, and it is analogical to TemporalCF.

- FCL
  - Federated Continual Learning breaks static limitations of FL; each client learns a task sequence
  - fundamental problem: spatial-temporal catastrophic forgetting
  - clients: TemporalCF from new tasks; server: SpatialCF from aggregation
  - after each task: server aggregates -> global model -> foundation for next task => SpatialCF may exacerbate TemporalCF
- This survey
  - enumerate FCL algorithms, how they overcome spatial/temporal CF or both
  - extensive experiments; FCL training = knowledge fusion (previous + current task; heterogeneous clients)
  - uploading full parameters/gradients: privacy leakage, slow aggregation from communication cost
  - FCL methods: extract knowledge locally, upload extracted knowledge, more efficient aggregation
  - contributions: discuss FCL, spatial-temporal CF, two evaluation metrics, experiments; two unified frameworks (synchronous, asynchronous); survey by seven forms of knowledge fusion (rehearsal, clustering, regularization, parameter isolation, dynamic architecture, prototype, knowledge distillation)
- Organization
  - Sec. II: FL, CL, motivation for FCL
  - Sec. III: spatial-temporal CF, experiments on traditional FL
  - Sec. IV: synchronous and asynchronous FCL frameworks
  - Sec. V: FCL methods by knowledge fusion (rehearsal, clustering, all gradients/parameters, parameter isolation, prototype, dynamic architecture, knowledge distillation)
  - Sec. VI: summary, future directions

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Deep learning has been instrumental in the advances of data analysis and artificial intelligence (AI). The algorithms have been used successfully in almost all application areas in industry, science, and engineering. However, traditional deep learning algorithms usually need large amounts of training data and centralized training, and this is often impractical or even impossible in practice. For example, with mobile devices it is difficult to collect large amounts of data and transfer them to a central server with limited bandwidth. Centralized training is also infeasible because of data privacy and data silos, which come from information security, related laws and regulations, and intensive competition among technology giants. In recent years federated learning (FL) has emerged as a positive response to the increasing need for privacy and other concerns in machine learning applications. In this new paradigm, multiple devices train a global model collaboratively by uploading their models to a server while the private data stays local, instead of the traditional approach with centralized data storage and model training. FL mainly involves privacy preservation, knowledge transfer, and collaboration among data owners, and these are essential for many real-world applications of AI. After several years of development FL has produced promising results, especially in industries that handle sensitive data such as finance, healthcare, electronic communication and government affairs.

FL has many advantages but it also faces significant challenges. The first challenge is that it lacks dynamism. Most existing FL methods make quite strong assumptions, namely that all data and classes are known beforehand and will never change. This contradicts the dynamic nature of the real world, where data is collected in streams and the data can form sequential tasks. But traditional FL would suffer from terrible temporal catastrophic forgetting (TemporalCF) when the local models learn new tasks. TemporalCF is a major challenge in Continual Learning (CL); it refers to changes in crucial parameters of a single model when it learns on consecutive tasks, which leads to poor performance on previous tasks. So FL would certainly run into TemporalCF if each client learns a sequence of tasks from a private local data stream.

Another challenge of FL is data heterogeneity, which is also called non-independent and identically distributed (Non-IID) data. It means the differences in data distributions, feature spaces and labels across the clients in the federated training process, caused by variations in the data sources, data collection methods, data quality, etc. Because of data heterogeneity, the local models extract diverse knowledge. The knowledge of a model is often represented by its parameters, and the more different the data is, the greater the parameter divergence is. If we simply aggregate these local models, for example by averaging parameters, parameters that are critical for some local tasks can be overwritten. So the aggregated global model may perform worse than the local models on the local test set. We call this phenomenon spatial catastrophic forgetting (SpatialCF). SpatialCF is a new concept that we introduce in this paper, and it is analogical to TemporalCF.

Federated Continual Learning (FCL) breaks the static limitations of traditional federated learning, with each client learning a task sequence. Beyond FL and CL, FCL has a fundamental problem called spatial-temporal catastrophic forgetting. On the local side, the clients need to overcome TemporalCF caused by learning new tasks. On the server side, the server has to deal with SpatialCF caused by aggregating different local models. After the training of a task is finished, the server aggregates the local models into a global model, and then the clients use the global model as a foundational model for continual learning of the next task. So SpatialCF may make TemporalCF worse.

In this paper, we go through several FCL algorithms in depth to explore how they overcome spatial or temporal catastrophic forgetting, or both. We evaluate them with extensive experiments and we show that the training process of FCL is basically a sort of knowledge fusion: fusing the knowledge of previous tasks with the knowledge of the current task, and also fusing heterogeneous knowledge from different clients. Uploading all the local parameters or gradients to the server may cause privacy leakages and slow down the aggregation because of the large communication cost, so FCL methods typically extract knowledge during local training, upload the extracted local knowledge and explore more efficient model aggregation strategies.

The main contributions of this paper are:

- We discuss FCL thoroughly. We raise the problem of spatial-temporal CF. We also define two evaluation metrics and do extensive experiments to evaluate the effect of spatial-temporal CF on FCL.

- We propose two unified frameworks for FCL (synchronous and asynchronous FCL). The two frameworks can integrate most existing methods and give two pipelines for future research.

- We give a comprehensive survey of existing FCL methods, categorizing them by seven forms of knowledge fusion: rehearsal, clustering, regularization, parameter isolation, dynamic architecture, prototype and knowledge distillation.

The rest of the paper is organized as follows. Sec. II gives an overview of FL and CL and discusses the motivation for combining them, i.e., FCL. Sec. III introduces the problem of spatial-temporal catastrophic forgetting and shows through experiments the weaknesses of traditional FL for this problem. Sec. IV presents two generic FCL frameworks: synchronous FCL and asynchronous FCL. Sec. V goes into various FCL methods and categorizes them by the forms of knowledge fusion, namely rehearsal, clustering, all gradients/parameters, parameter isolation, prototype, dynamic architecture and knowledge distillation. Sec. VI briefly summarizes the survey and highlights some potential directions for future work in FCL.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Deep learning has been instrumental in the advances of both data analysis and artificial intelligence (AI) [1]. The algorithms have also been successfully used in almost all areas of applications in industry, science, and engineering [2]. However, traditional deep learning algorithms often require large amounts of training data and centralized training, which are usually impractical or even impossible in practical situations. For example, in the case of mobile devices, it is difficult to collect large amounts of data and transfer them to a central server with limited bandwidth [3]. Centralized training is also infeasible due to data privacy and data silos, which arise from information security, related laws and regulations, and intensive competition among technology giants [4]. In recent years, federated learning (FL) has emerged as a positive response to the increasing need for privacy and other concerns in machine learning applications [5]. This newly emerging paradigm deploys multiple devices to train a global model collaboratively by uploading their models to a server while keeping the private data locally, as opposed to the traditional approach of centralized data storage and model training. FL mainly involves privacy preservation, knowledge transfer, and collaboration among data owners, which are essential for many real-world applications of AI. After several years of development, FL has produced promising results, particularly in industries that handle sensitive data such as finance, healthcare, electronic communication and government affairs [6,7,8].

Despite its numerous advantages, FL confronts significant challenges. The first challenge is the lack of dynamism. The assumptions of most existing FL methods are somewhat strong: all data and classes are assumed to be known in advance and to remain unchanged forever. This contradicts the dynamic nature of the real world, where data are collected in streams and could form sequential tasks. Traditional FL would therefore suffer from terrible temporal catastrophic forgetting (TemporalCF) when local models learn new tasks. TemporalCF is a major challenge in Continual Learning (CL) [9], which refers to changes in crucial parameters of a single model when learning on consecutive tasks, resulting in poor performance on previous tasks [10]. Clearly, FL would encounter TemporalCF if each client learns on a sequence of tasks from a private local data stream.

Another challenge of FL is data heterogeneity [4], also known as non-independent and identically distributed (Non-IID) data. It refers to the differences in data distributions, feature spaces and labels across the clients participating in the federated training process, caused by variations in the data sources, data collection methods, data quality, etc. Data heterogeneity results in diverse knowledge being extracted by local models. The knowledge of a model is often represented by its parameters, and the more different the data, the greater the parameter divergence. Simply aggregating these local models, e.g., by averaging parameters, can lead to critical parameters for certain local tasks being overwritten, so that the aggregated global model may perform worse than the local models on the local test set [11,12,13]. We call this phenomenon spatial catastrophic forgetting (SpatialCF). Note that SpatialCF is a new concept we introduce in this paper, analogical to TemporalCF.

Federated Continual Learning (FCL) [14,15] breaks the static limitations of traditional federated learning, with each client learning a task sequence. Beyond FL and CL, FCL has a fundamental problem called spatial-temporal catastrophic forgetting. On the local side, clients need to overcome TemporalCF induced by learning new tasks. On the server side, the server must address SpatialCF caused by aggregating different local models. Specifically, after the training of a task is completed, the server aggregates local models into a global model, and the clients then use the global model as a foundational model for continual learning of the next task. Therefore, SpatialCF may exacerbate TemporalCF.

In this paper, we enumerate several FCL algorithms in depth to explore how they overcome spatial or temporal catastrophic forgetting, or both. We evaluate them with extensive experiments and show that the training process of FCL is essentially a sort of knowledge fusion: fusing the knowledge of previous tasks with the current task's knowledge, as well as fusing heterogeneous knowledge from different clients. Specifically, since uploading the entire local parameters or gradients to the server may cause privacy leakages [16,17] and slow down the aggregation due to the large communication cost [18,19], FCL methods typically extract knowledge during local training, upload the extracted local knowledge and explore more efficient model aggregation strategies.

The main contributions of this paper are summarized as follows:

- We discuss FCL thoroughly in this work and raise the problem of spatial-temporal CF. We further define two evaluation metrics and conduct extensive experiments to evaluate the effect of spatial-temporal CF on FCL.

- We propose two unified frameworks for FCL (i.e., synchronous and asynchronous FCL). The two frameworks can integrate most existing methods and lay two pipelines for future research.

- We present a comprehensive survey of existing FCL methods by categorizing them with seven forms of knowledge fusion, namely rehearsal, clustering, regularization, parameter isolation, dynamic architecture, prototype and knowledge distillation.

The rest of this paper is organized as follows. In Sec. II, we provide an overview of FL and CL and discuss the motivation for their integration, i.e., FCL. In Sec. III, we introduce the problem of spatial-temporal catastrophic forgetting and demonstrate the weaknesses of traditional FL for this problem through experiments. In Sec. IV, we present two generic FCL frameworks: synchronous FCL and asynchronous FCL. In Sec. V, we look into various FCL methods and categorize them according to the forms of knowledge fusion, namely rehearsal, clustering, all gradients/parameters, parameter isolation, prototype, dynamic architecture and knowledge distillation. In Sec. VI, we briefly summarize our survey and highlight some potential research directions for future work in FCL.
